messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martha was 68 when the ceiling of the community center collapsed during a holiday dinner. She had been standing near the dessert table, holding a plate of her famous pecan pie, when the old wooden beams gave way with a sound like a cannon shot. She remembered the smell of splintered pine and spilled wine, the way a woman’s scream seemed to come from everywhere at once. For a long moment, she was pinned beneath a fallen beam, her cheek pressed against the cold linoleum, her left arm twisted beneath her. She could hear people shouting, could feel the weight of the debris on her back, and what she remembered most vividly—what she could still see, years later, as though it were a photograph projected onto the inside of her eyelids—was the pattern of the ceiling tiles above her, a grid of tiny holes, just before everything went dark. She had been an artist all her life, a painter of landscapes and still lifes, and that image had burned itself into her visual memory with a permanence she could not shake.

In the months that followed, Martha found that the memory came with a physical reenactment she could not control. Whenever the recollection surfaced, her body would stiffen into that same pinned position, her left arm pressing against her ribs, her cheek tilting toward an invisible floor. And with the memory came a crushing guilt: she had been the one to suggest the venue, had insisted that the community center was perfect for the dinner. She had convinced her husband, who had been reluctant to attend, and he had been standing only a few feet away when the beam fell. He had survived, but the guilt had not faded with time. She had come to believe that her judgment was fundamentally flawed, that the world was a place where ceilings fell without warning, where her own choices could bring harm to the people she loved. Her beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed. She was not sure her life was worth living anymore, and she had begun to feel that she would never be able to feel normal emotions again.

Martha worked from a studio in her home, a converted garage where she had painted for forty years. But the studio had become a place of vigilance rather than creation. She would be mixing paint on her palette when a creak from the roof would make her freeze, her heart hammering, her eyes fixed on the ceiling. She had started listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering her home, even during the day, even when she knew she was alone. Sleep had become fragmented; she would lie awake in the dark, tracking the groan of the house settling, certain that the ceiling was about to give way. Her therapist had noted that Martha’s irritability had grown—she snapped at neighbors who knocked unexpectedly, and she had ended a phone call with her daughter by shouting, then hanging up, then crying for an hour.

The triggers were everywhere, and each one pulled her back into the memory. The smell of alcohol on a passerby’s breath—someone walking past her on the sidewalk—would bring the image of spilled wine on linoleum, and she would feel her body stiffen, her arm pressing against her ribs. Physical touch, even a hand on her shoulder from a well-meaning friend, made her flinch and pull away, because her body remembered the weight of the beam. And crying—she had started to cry at unexpected moments, and the sight of her own tears in the mirror would trigger the memory of the woman’s scream, and she would feel the guilt wash over her again, and she would become convinced that she would never feel normal emotions, which only made her cry harder.

She had developed a set of strategies to manage the chaos. She tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the images away whenever they began to surface, but the suppression required constant effort. She kept her mind occupied all the time—she listened to audiobooks while she painted, she watched television while she ate, she played word games on her phone while she waited for water to boil. She avoided news reports about building collapses or natural disasters, changing the channel or leaving the room if a story came on. But the avoidance had narrowed her world. She no longer visited restaurants with high ceilings. She had stopped going to the grocery store because the overhead lights, suspended on wires, reminded her of the community center. Her daughter had started doing her shopping, and Martha was grateful, but she was also ashamed.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in late November, three years after the collapse. She had been standing in her studio, brush in hand, staring at a blank canvas, when she heard a car backfire in the street. The sound was distant and ordinary, but her body had reacted as though the ceiling were falling again. She had dropped the brush, had pressed herself against the wall, had felt her left arm curl against her ribs, and when the moment passed, she had stood there shaking, unable to pick up the brush. She was afraid that she was losing the ability to paint, the one thing that had given her life meaning. She was afraid that her life was not worth living. But she was also, for the first time, willing to say that out loud.
